title: How to Secure Agents using OAuth — Jared Hanson (Keycard, Passport.js)

primary.label: AI Platforms & Developer Tooling
primary.rationale: The talk focuses on securing AI agents via OAuth, identity management, and MCP authorization protocols.

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk focuses on securing AI agents via OAuth, identity management, and MCP authorization protocols.

summary: Jared Hanson opens by framing a critical tension in AI agent security: connected agents are more useful, but giving them broad, long-lived API keys creates serious security problems at scale. He positions OAuth as the established solution for replacing static secrets with dynamic, scoped access tokens. He provides a primer on OAuth: clients request access to resource servers (APIs), mediated by an authorization server that issues tokens after user consent. Refresh tokens enable short-lived access tokens with persistent connections. He clarifies the common confusion between OAuth (authorization) and sign-in (authentication), explaining that OpenID Connect formalized the sign-in pattern as an identity layer on top of OAuth, introducing ID tokens as signed JWTs. The three OAuth roles—client, resource server, authorization server—centralize authentication and policy at the authorization server, freeing APIs from auth concerns. Turning to MCP, Hanson traces its authorization history: the initial spec had no auth ("NOAuth"), the March draft incorrectly collapsed the authorization server role into the MCP server, prompting viral criticism from Christian Posta and Aaron Perky. The latest draft fixes this by making the OAuth authorization server a separate entity. Hanson then addresses agent identity challenges. MCP uses dynamic client registration, but this 10-year-old spec has seen no meaningful adoption and makes agents anonymous via uncredentialed registration requests, undermining trust. He suggests push client registration for public clients and proposes using URLs with PKI for verifiable agent identity, authenticating agents through cryptographic signatures. He discusses agent attestation—awareness of which LLM receives agent data—and points to IETF work on remote attestation. For transactional authorization, he notes scopes are too coarse-grained for financial transactions and recommends rich authorization requests. He addresses chain of custody: MCP covers agent-to-server connections but leaves server-to-API calls unspecified, recommending OAuth token exchange and the identity assertion grant for cross-domain authorization. He raises async interaction challenges—users walking away while agents work—and voice/video security, citing prior art in SIP, XMPP, and WebRTC. Hanson concludes by introducing Keycard, an identity access management platform for connecting agents to apps and infrastructure using OAuth, OpenID Connect, and MCP.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.
temporalContext: Transcript claims reflect the publication date; linked external context was checked at the run's research date.
takeaways: Sharing long-lived, broadly-scoped API keys with agents creates severe security problems at scale; OAuth replaces static secrets with dynamic, scoped access tokens.
OAuth has three roles—client, resource server, and authorization server—with the authorization server mediating access by issuing tokens.

The first MCP spec had no authorization; the March draft incorrectly collapsed the authorization server into the MCP server, drawing widespread criticism; the latest draft properly separates these roles.
Dynamic client registration, used by MCP, has seen no meaningful adoption in 10 years and makes agents anonymous due to uncredentialed registration requests, undermining trust.
Push client registration offers a simpler alternative for public clients using well-known strings, avoiding the registration and state storage overhead.
Hanson proposes using URLs and PKI for agent identity, authenticating agents via cryptographic signatures (JWT assertions or HTTP message signatures) verifiable with public keys.
OAuth scopes are too coarse-grained and long-lived for transactional agent use cases like financial transactions; rich authorization requests offer more dynamic, transaction-level access.
MCP does not specify the security profile for MCP servers calling other APIs; OAuth token exchange and the identity assertion grant address chain-of-custody and cross-domain authorization.
Agent attestation—knowing which LLM receives agent data—is an emerging concern, with IETF work on remote attestation applicable to edge-deployed agents.
Async agent interaction requires rethinking OAuth's browser-centric assumptions, incorporating SMS or push notifications for real-time permission requests.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Hanson introduces himself as co-founder of Keycard, creator of Passport.js, and formerly of Auth0 and Okta. He frames the core tension: connected agents are more useful, but today we face an impossible choice between broad access with security risk or limited capabilities with sacrificed business value. Current MCP setup uses long-lived, broadly-scoped API keys pasted into config files—a pattern that doesn't scale securely.

sections.title: OAuth Fundamentals
sections.summary: Hanson introduces OAuth as a protocol where clients request access to resource servers (APIs), mediated by an authorization server. Using the Calendly-Google Calendar example, he explains consent flows, access tokens, and refresh tokens that allow short-lived access tokens to be rotated while maintaining authorized connections. Authorization code flows involve user delegation via browser-based interfaces.

sections.title: OAuth vs Sign-in and OpenID Connect
sections.summary: Hanson clarifies the common confusion around OAuth being used for sign-in. 'Sign in with Google' is a special case where the API is a user info API returning user claims. This pattern was formalized as OpenID Connect, an identity layer on top of OAuth that standardizes user info response format, introduces ID tokens (signed JWTs), and adds terminology like identity provider and relying party.

sections.title: OAuth Roles and Benefits
sections.summary: Hanson emphasizes OAuth's three roles: client, resource server, and authorization server. The authorization server mediates access by issuing tokens. The main benefit flows to APIs—they no longer handle authentication, password verification, or consent flows. Policy can be centralized, enabling ecosystems of apps and APIs protected by a central authorization server.

sections.title: Applying OAuth to MCP
sections.summary: Hanson maps the OAuth model onto MCP: chatbots or agents (MCP clients) connect to MCP servers, with both authorized via OAuth through a controlling authorization server in the middle. He notes that nothing with OAuth is ever simple.

sections.title: State of Authorization in MCP: History and Fixes
sections.summary: Hanson traces MCP authorization history. The first version ('NOAuth') had no authorization. The March draft incorrectly required MCP servers to implement the full authorization server role, collapsing two OAuth roles into one. This drew viral criticism from Christian Posta and Aaron Perky, and generated PRs with hundreds of comments. Hanson notes he had recommended modeling MCP servers as resource servers back in January.

sections.title: Latest MCP Draft and Future Directions
sections.summary: The latest MCP draft properly separates the OAuth authorization server as a distinct entity, simplifying MCP server implementation to token verification. Hanson previews future needs: agent-to-agent communication using client credentials flow (agents acting on their own behalf rather than delegating user access), and the emerging question of agent identity, paralleling developer portal workflows for obtaining client IDs and secrets.

sections.title: Agent Identity: Dynamic Client Registration and Alternatives
sections.summary: Hanson explains that MCP uses dynamic client registration, allowing agents to request credentials at runtime. However, this 10-year-old spec has seen no meaningful adoption and makes agents anonymous due to uncredentialed registration requests, undermining trust. For public clients, he recommends push client registration, which uses well-known strings to skip registration entirely. For clients requiring verified identity, he proposes using URLs and PKI—agents authenticate by signing JWT assertions or HTTP message signatures verifiable with corresponding public keys.

sections.title: Agent Attestation
sections.summary: Hanson raises the issue that agents send data to LLMs, requiring awareness and control. In protected environments, the LLM can be treated as another API, but this doesn't work for edge-deployed agents on desktop or mobile. He points to IETF work on remote attestation and supply chain security to attest to device and software state, enabling authorization flows that know which LLM receives agent data.

sections.title: Transactional Authorization
sections.summary: Hanson notes OAuth scopes are better than passwords but too coarse-grained and long-lived for many agent use cases. For financial or commercial transactions, agents need transaction-level authorization with specific amounts or budgets. He recommends the rich authorization requests specification for more dynamic, transaction-based access control.

sections.title: Chain of Custody and Agent-to-Agent Flows
sections.summary: Hanson explains MCP only covers the first leg—agent to MCP server connections. The right side, where MCP servers call other APIs, is unspecified. He recommends OAuth token exchange for same-domain calls and the identity assertion grant for cross-domain identity chaining. He envisions agent-to-agent flows where graphs of agents communicate across servers, requiring end-to-end visibility of authorization along these chains.

sections.title: Async and Voice/Video Interaction Security
sections.summary: Hanson notes OAuth assumes a user at a browser, but agents work asynchronously in the background. Users may walk away, and agents need ways to request additional access via SMS or push notifications rather than browser-only flows. He also raises voice and video interaction security as a frontier, citing prior art in SIP, XMPP, and WebRTC communities.

sections.title: Conclusion and Keycard
sections.summary: Hanson summarizes the breadth of work needed for a safe and secure AI future. He introduces Keycard as an identity access management platform connecting co-pilots, custom agents, and third-party agents to apps, services, and infrastructure using standards-compliant protocols: OpenID Connect, MCP, and OAuth. Keycard is hiring and seeking partners building agents to work with on security.

limitations: The MCP authorization specification as of the March draft gave a misinformed view of OAuth
OAuth is a relatively complicated protocol, especially considering all extensions
Current OAuth-in-MCP coverage only scratches the surface of what is needed to fully secure AI interactions
Dynamic client registration makes agents anonymous due to uncredentialed registration requests, making it hard to build trust
OAuth scopes are too coarse-grained and long-lived for transactional agent use cases
MCP does not specify the security profile for MCP servers calling other APIs within or across domains
OAuth typically assumes a user sitting in front of a browser, which doesn't fit async agent workflows
Treating LLMs as just another API has limited applicability for edge-deployed agents on desktop or mobile devices
